newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end little changed, await new supply.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end little changed, await new supply.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended little changed as players were sidelined, awaiting the first leg of the Treasury's quarterly refunding effort, analysts said.

"The market doesn't have anything to focus on of significance on the economic front, so it's really: how is supply going to go?," said Mead Briggs, head of U.S. government proprietary trading at Credit Suisse First Boston.
Traders said talk of leveraged funds selling 10-year Treasury notes and central banks offering the five-year issue put some downward pressure on the market in early trade.
"Dealers kind of pulled in their horns because of the refunding. At the same time there was talk of selling of fives and 10s," said Josh Stiles, bond strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc.

After touching a low yield of 6.88 percent, its lowest in more than a month on Friday, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond slipped 14/32 in early trade on Monday. It traded steadily near the low during the morning, before recouping most of its losses at midafternoon.
The T-bond closed down 1/32 at 96-25/32, yielding 6.88 percent. The results from the Treasury's weekly bill auctions on Monday may have helped the market's tone, analysts said.

The Treasury sold three-month bills at 5.14 percent with no tail and a 8.94 bid-to-cover ratio. Six-month bills were auctioned at 5.37 percent, also with a zero-basis-point tail, and bids exceeded the amount auctioned by 6.22 times.
The 3-month bill rate ended off 10 basis points at 5.00 percent and the 6-month fell one basis point to 5.31 percent.
But the weekly tender was just a sideshow to the main event, which kicks off Tuesday with the auction of $17 billion in three-year notes and concludes with $12 billion in ten-year notes on Wednesday.

With no 30-year paper to absorb and future prospects for even less paper in the market, once the details of the Washington budget agreement are hammered out and approved by Congress, dealers said the market should not have a hard time swallowing the supply of new paper.

"The Treasury is just so flush with cash it helped the budget deficit talks too, because they can use higher assumptions. The amount they have to issue in the immediate future is less than had been expected," said Briggs.
"I mean you've got lots of things that are all working for the market. But we're going to have some sort of consolidation with supply," Briggs said.
Some analysts said they were concerned the recent bond rally might have gotten ahead of itself before the refunding.

"The three-year is at (6-3/8 percent) already," said Maria Fiorini Ramirez, president and CEO at MFR Inc. "Let's hope it doesn't get stronger. A three-year with a 6.25 coupon, I don't think it would be too good."
The three-year note ended down 2/32 at 98-23/32. The yield rose to 6.38 percent from 6.36 percent on Friday.
Experts also said an explosive late rise on Wall Street on Monday might have played a roll in propping up the bonds during the U.S. afternoon.
The Dow Jones industrials average ended 142.48 points higher on Monday.
"It looks to me like they really came back together, beginning right about two oclock (1400 EDT)," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
March U.S. factory orders, due at 1000 EDT on Tuesday, are not expected to be a significant factor in trade, having already been previewed in last week's durable goods data.
